clusters.label: Keras definition and purpose
clusters.rationale: These candidates describe what Keras is (high-level API, simplifies neural networks) and its purpose, acting as an introductory definition.

clusters.label: Keras backend flexibility and ecosystem
clusters.rationale: Both candidates discuss the backend engines supported by Keras and its integration with TensorFlow, focusing on the technical flexibility.

clusters.label: Keras model types (Sequential and Functional)
clusters.rationale: These candidates introduce the two main model types in Keras: Sequential for linear stacks and Functional for complex architectures.

clusters.label: Building Sequential model with Dense layers
clusters.rationale: Both candidates describe constructing a Sequential model by stacking Dense layers, specifying units and activation functions, with code examples.

clusters.label: Compiling a Keras model
clusters.rationale: These candidates cover the compilation step (model.compile()), explaining the need for loss, optimizer, and metrics, with examples for different tasks.

clusters.label: Training a Keras model with model.fit
clusters.rationale: All candidates describe the training process using model.fit(), highlighting parameters like epochs, batch_size, and validation_data, and illustrating with code.

clusters.label: Evaluating a trained model on test data
clusters.rationale: These candidates demonstrate model.evaluate() to compute loss and accuracy on test data, providing unbiased performance metrics.

clusters.label: Making predictions with Keras models
clusters.rationale: These candidates show how to generate predictions using model.predict() and interpret the output (e.g., using np.argmax) for classification or regression tasks.

clusters.label: Image preprocessing: normalization
clusters.rationale: Both candidates explain dividing pixel values by 255 to normalize grayscale images to [0,1] for improved training, a standard preprocessing step for image data.

clusters.label: Image preprocessing: reshaping and Flatten layer
clusters.rationale: These candidates discuss preparing image data for Dense layers by reshaping 2D images to 1D vectors, either manually via .reshape() or using a Flatten layer in the model.

clusters.label: One-hot encoding for categorical labels
clusters.rationale: Both candidates detail converting integer labels to one-hot encoded vectors using to_categorical for multi-class classification tasks.

clusters.label: Keras model inspection
clusters.rationale: These candidates describe how to retrieve model information using methods like summary(), output_shape, get_config(), and get_weights() after defining the architecture.

clusters.label: Saving and reloading Keras models
clusters.rationale: These candidates explain persisting a trained model with model.save() and restoring it with load_model(), enabling reuse and deployment.

clusters.label: Fine-tuning with optimizer parameters
clusters.rationale: These candidates describe customizing optimizer instances (e.g., RMSprop with learning rate and decay) to fine-tune training behavior.

clusters.label: Fine-tuning with Early Stopping
clusters.rationale: These candidates explain using the EarlyStopping callback to prevent overfitting by halting training when a monitored metric stops improving.

clusters.label: End-to-end Keras workflow for classification
clusters.rationale: These candidates outline the complete pipeline from defining the network to making predictions, emphasizing a structured workflow that can be applied to classification tasks.

clusters.label: Loading built-in Keras datasets
clusters.rationale: These candidates demonstrate loading standard datasets like MNIST, CIFAR-10, Boston Housing, and IMDb from tensorflow.keras.datasets, including code for unpacking into train/test sets.

clusters.label: MNIST dataset characteristics and loading
clusters.rationale: These candidates specifically focus on the MNIST dataset: its properties (28x28 images, 10 digits, train/test split) and how to load it using keras.datasets.mnist.load_data().

clusters.label: Inspecting data shape and labels
clusters.rationale: Both candidates describe checking array shapes and inspecting labels after loading data, often using print statements and visualization (e.g., plt.matshow).

clusters.label: Sequence padding for RNNs
clusters.rationale: These candidates cover the preprocessing step of padding sequences to a fixed length using pad_sequences, essential for feeding variable-length data into RNNs.

clusters.label: Train/test split with sklearn
clusters.rationale: These candidates describe using sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split to partition data into training and test sets, controlling test_size and random_state.

clusters.label: Standardization with StandardScaler
clusters.rationale: These candidates explain fitting a StandardScaler to training data and transforming both train and test sets to have zero mean and unit variance, a common preprocessing step.

clusters.label: Building an MLP for binary classification
clusters.rationale: Both candidates show constructing a Sequential model with Dense layers using relu for hidden layers and sigmoid for the output layer, tailored for binary classification tasks.

clusters.label: Building an MLP for multi-class classification with Dropout
clusters.rationale: These candidates illustrate stacking Dense layers with relu activation, interspersed with Dropout layers, and a softmax output layer for multi-class problems.

clusters.label: Building an MLP for regression
clusters.rationale: These candidates describe creating a regression neural network with Dense layers where the output layer omits activation to predict continuous values.

clusters.label: Building a CNN in Keras
clusters.rationale: These candidates outline constructing a convolutional neural network with Conv2D, Activation, MaxPooling2D, Dropout, Flatten, and Dense layers, a standard CNN architecture.

clusters.label: Building an RNN with LSTM
clusters.rationale: These candidates describe building a recurrent network with an Embedding layer, an LSTM layer with dropout, and a Dense output for binary classification on sequential data.

clusters.label: Loading external data from URL
clusters.rationale: These candidates show how to fetch a dataset from a URL using urllib and np.loadtxt, a technique for loading external CSV data into NumPy arrays for training.

clusters.label: Keras on Kaggle Kernels (no local setup)
clusters.rationale: These candidates explain using Kaggle Kernels as a cloud environment with Keras pre-installed, eliminating local installation steps and offering immediate practice.

clusters.label: TensorFlow definition and history
clusters.rationale: These candidates introduce TensorFlow: open-source ML platform by Google, its computational graph approach, origin from Google Brain, and its release timeline.

clusters.label: TensorFlow ecosystem and components
clusters.rationale: These candidates discuss the broader TensorFlow ecosystem, including TF.js, TF Lite, TFX, and other tools, emphasizing flexibility and deployment options.

clusters.label: TensorBoard visualization tool
clusters.rationale: These candidates describe TensorBoard as a suite of visualization tools for monitoring and debugging ML models, often used alongside TensorFlow.

clusters.label: TensorFlow Hub pre-trained models
clusters.rationale: These candidates explain TensorFlow Hub as a repository of reusable pre-trained models, simplifying transfer learning and model deployment.

clusters.label: Machine learning model definition
clusters.rationale: These candidates define what a machine learning model is (a file trained on data to recognize patterns) and its role in making predictions.

clusters.label: TensorFlow Playground
clusters.rationale: These candidates introduce TensorFlow Playground as an interactive web-based tool for experimenting with neural networks, useful for learning.

clusters.label: TensorFlow competitors (PyTorch, etc.)
clusters.rationale: These candidates list major alternatives to TensorFlow (e.g., PyTorch, CNTK, MXNet) and briefly compare their strengths, providing context in the ML landscape.

clusters.label: TensorFlow in industry applications
clusters.rationale: These candidates give real-world examples of TensorFlow usage by companies (Google, PayPal, Twitter, GE), illustrating its practical impact.

clusters.label: TensorFlow Quantum
clusters.rationale: These candidates mention TensorFlow Quantum (TFQ), a library for combining quantum computing with machine learning, announced in 2020.

clusters.label: Becoming an ML specialist
clusters.rationale: These candidates outline the four pillars for becoming an ML specialist (programming, math, theory, practice) and mention the TensorFlow Developer Certificate.

clusters.label: TensorFlow CPU/GPU package installation
clusters.rationale: These candidates detail installing TensorFlow via pip, covering packages for CPU, GPU Linux, and GPU Windows, and verifying installation with test commands.

clusters.label: NVIDIA GPU dependencies for TensorFlow
clusters.rationale: These candidates list the required NVIDIA software (driver, CUDA Toolkit, cuDNN) and versions for GPU support, including the optional TensorRT.

clusters.label: GPU support by OS and Windows-specific setup
clusters.rationale: These candidates cover the OS limitations (no GPU on macOS, restrictions on Windows), recommend Miniconda for Windows, and mention the Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable dependency.

clusters.label: System requirements for TensorFlow
clusters.rationale: These candidates specify the supported operating systems, Python versions, and pip versions for TensorFlow installation, providing a prerequisites checklist.

clusters.label: GPU memory management in TensorFlow
clusters.rationale: These candidates explain TensorFlow's default aggressive GPU memory allocation, how to set fixed memory limits, enable memory growth, and monitor usage with nvidia-smi and profiling tools.
